title: Twenty-Five Years of Progress Against Child Stunting in Rwanda (2000–2025): Trends, Socioeconomic Inequalities, and Progress Toward National and Global Targets
content: Rwanda has set one of the most ambitious national stunting targets in sub-Saharan Africa of 15% by 2029 under the second National Strategy for Transformation, NST2, and the World Health Assembly has extended the global nutrition targets to 2030. We pooled the children’s recode files of six Rwanda Demographic and Health Surveys from 2000–2025; 48,735 children, 28,077 with valid anthropometry, recomputed WHO-2006 z-scores from raw measurements for all rounds (99.7% agreement with DHS values at the −2 SD cut-off), and estimated design-based prevalences, average annual rates of reduction (AARR), slope and relative indices of inequality, concentration indices, provincial trends, adjusted prevalence ratios from modified-Poisson models and log-linear projections to 2029–2050. Stunting fell from 47.7% in 2000 (peak 51.4% in 2005) to 26.6% in 2025, with the AARR accelerating to 4.1%/year over 2019–2025; severe stunting fell from 23.0% to 6.1%. Prevalence at 0–5 months was unchanged (17.4% to 16.3%). Progress was steeply pro-rich: stunting fell from 33.4% to 8.9% in the richest quintile but only from 51.3% to 39.3% in the poorest, and the relative index of inequality rose from 1.51 to 4.06. The Northern and Western provinces remained at 33% versus 14% in Kigali. On the 2010–2025 trajectory, stunting would be 23.8% in 2029; reaching 15% requires an AARR of 14.7%/year, four times the current pace, whereas the WHA/SDG-2030 prevalence-equivalent (22–26%) is attainable. Meeting the NST2 target will require a step-change in the coverage and equity of maternal nutrition, early-life and poverty-graduation interventions.
